_about: Implementations, each resolved against its registry before being written down. Five registries are used, because restricting the check to npm and PyPI restricted the catalogue to JavaScript and Python.
_method: Every row resolved with a 200 from its registry: registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json, crates.io/api/v1/crates, api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer, or api.github.com/repos for the C++ and shader libraries that live only on GitHub. Six original candidates 404ed and were dropped; five more resolved to unrelated projects sharing a name — PyPI `sdf` is Scientific Data Format, `wfc` is WebForms Core — and were dropped too. The same trap caught two more during the expansion pass: PyPI `pymo` is MongoClient instrumentation, not motion capture, and PyPI `meep` is a task runner, not the MIT photonics solver. All 71 original rows were then re-resolved in full: none had disappeared and no version had moved.
_caveat:
Version, licence and release date are the registry's answer, not a judgement. Two caveats worth carrying:

First, four GitHub-hosted rows have no SPDX licence identifier — OpenSubdiv, CGAL, mxgmn's WaveFunctionCollapse and lygia all carry terms that GitHub cannot classify automatically. Read the repository before shipping any of them.

Second, one row is listed despite being unmaintained: Accord.Math has had no release since 2017, and is here because a large amount of existing C# generation code depends on it. That is recorded rather than hidden.

_roles.output-surface: Turns generated data into something perceivable.
_roles.model: A learned model, called rather than run.
_roles.authoring-app: A human opens it. Cannot be called from a server.
_roles.analysis: Analyses existing content. Feeds generation but does not generate.
_roles.infrastructure: Numerical or runtime substrate. Implements no generative algorithm itself.

implementations.description: Colour conversion, scales, interpolation and contrast. The most widely used palette-generation library in JavaScript, and the one that made "interpolate in Lab, not RGB" common practice.

Written by two editors of the CSS Color specification, which makes it the reference for what the spec means in practice: every space, CIEDE2000 and other difference formulas, gamut mapping, and both WCAG 2 and APCA contrast.

A tree-shakeable colour library covering every CSS Color 4 space including Oklab and Oklch, with difference metrics, gamut mapping and interpolation. The most complete implementation of the specification outside a browser engine.

The WCAG relative-luminance contrast ratio and its score thresholds, and nothing else. Listed because the calculation is small enough that a wrong implementation is common, and this one is the widely-checked reference.
A CSS Color 4-aligned Python library: Oklab and Oklch, gamut mapping, interpolation with the specification's hue-handling rules, and both contrast algorithms. The Python counterpart to colorjs.io.

Colour science in the full sense: every standard space and transform, all the CIE difference formulas, appearance models including CAM16, spectral computation and chromatic adaptation. Where you go when a library-level approximation is not enough.

implementations.description: Marching squares over a scalar grid, producing GeoJSON multipolygons, with density estimation to build the grid from points. This is the isoline half of the field concept, and the saddle-case resolution is handled explicitly.

The largest single collection of image-space operators: convolution, Sobel and Laplacian, bilateral filtering, morphology, distance transforms, seamless cloning by Poisson blending, and inpainting. Most of the filter concept, in one import.
Image processing over NumPy arrays, with the pieces the filter and texsyn concepts need: filters and morphology, marching cubes and marching squares, histogram matching, inpainting, and segmentation.

The navmesh generator behind a large share of shipped games: voxelise arbitrary level geometry, filter by slope and headroom, erode by agent radius, and emit walkable polygons. Detour is the query and crowd half.

The author of the priority-flood paper's own implementation: depression filling, D8 and D-infinity routing, flow accumulation, watershed labelling, all parallelised for large rasters.

Watershed delineation over a NumPy-backed grid: fill, resolve flats, flow direction, accumulation, catchment extraction and stream ordering. The most direct route from a heightfield to a river network in Python.

A half-edge triangle mesh with the traversal and edit operations that depend on it: split, collapse, flip, and connectivity queries. The data structure the mesh concept is about, in Rust.

The computational geometry library that takes exactness seriously: Delaunay in 2D and 3D, mesh generation with quality guarantees, straight skeletons, booleans, and the exact predicate kernels the rest of the field borrows. Dual-licensed GPL and commercial.
Header-only geometry processing: decimation, subdivision, parameterisation, distances, curvature, booleans. The C++ library the research literature is written against, with a Python wrapper on PyPI.
Quadric error decimation in a single readable header — the clearest short implementation of Garland and Heckbert, and the one most ports and bindings are derived from.

Simplification, vertex-cache and overdraw optimisation, meshlet building and vertex-stream compression. This is the step between "the generator produced a mesh" and "the mesh is fast", and it is what glTF pipelines use.
The Python bindings to libigl. Chosen by much of the geometry-processing literature for reproducing results, which makes it the fastest way to check a paper's claim about a mesh operation.

Scriptable access to MeshLab's several hundred filters: quadric decimation, subdivision schemes, Poisson reconstruction, remeshing, curvature and repair. The broadest single mesh toolbox reachable from Python.
State-of-the-art diffusion in PyTorch and JAX.

Tensors and Dynamic neural networks in Python with strong GPU acceleration
The Rust port of FastNoiseLite. Worth listing separately from the C++ original because it is the half that makes cross-language determinism usable from a Rust server or a WASM client.
A newer Rust noise crate built around a generator-adapter pipeline, so a whole terrain stack is one expression with the composition checked at compile time.

The established Rust noise crate: Perlin, simplex, value, Worley, plus a combinator graph of fBm, billow, ridged multifractal, turbulence and domain warping built as composable types rather than as parameters.

A single header per language implementing OpenSimplex2, Perlin, value and cellular noise plus fBm and domain warping. The reason it matters here is portability: the same noise, byte-identical, in C++, C#, Rust, GLSL, JavaScript and Python, which is what lets a server and a shader agree on a world.

Single-file public-domain C libraries. Relevant here for stb_perlin.h — Perlin, ridged, turbulence and fBm in about 150 lines with no dependencies — and stb_image_resize for filtered field resampling.

Ashima and Gustavson's GLSL noise functions: 2D/3D/4D simplex, classic Perlin and cellular, written with no texture lookups or uniform arrays so they run on any WebGL target. Almost every shader on Shadertoy that uses noise uses a copy of these.

Rust's standard randomness crate. Relevant here for what it makes explicit rather than what it computes: seedable generators are a separate type from the OS entropy source, and the distinction between reproducible and secure randomness is enforced at compile time.

Catmull–Clark and Loop with semi-sharp creases, hierarchical edits and GPU evaluation. Inside Maya, Blender and RenderMan, which makes it less one implementation than the de facto definition of what a subdivision surface is in production.
Catmull–Clark and a simple split modifier for three.js BufferGeometry, replacing the SubdivisionModifier that was removed from three.js itself.

Neural texture synthesis and remixing: extend a photographed material, make it seamless, or transfer its statistics to another image. The descendant of Portilla–Simoncelli with a learned feature space in place of the steerable pyramid. Note the AGPL licence.

implementations.description: The optimiser half of an adjoint inverse-design loop: MMA, SLSQP, CCSA and the rest, all taking a user-supplied gradient. Pair it with an automatic-differentiation or adjoint-capable simulator and you have the machinery the nanophotonics literature uses.

NASA's multidisciplinary optimisation framework. Its reason to be here is analytic derivatives across coupled solvers: it assembles the adjoint for a whole system rather than for one simulation, which is what makes inverse design tractable when the physics has several parts.

A direct Python translation of the 88-line SIMP reference code — density variables, optimality-criteria update, sensitivity filter, finite elements. Recorded honestly: an early alpha by one author, listed because it is the only installable implementation of the textbook method and because the method is short enough that the code is the specification.

The Rust port of Delaunator: incremental Delaunay triangulation with a space-filling-curve insertion order, from which the Voronoi dual falls out. Fast enough that the triangulation stops being the bottleneck.

Delaunay and constrained Delaunay triangulations with exact predicates and refinement to a quality bound. The constrained half is what you need when the triangulation has to respect a coastline or a road you already generated.

_resolved: The previous version of this file observed that many npm packages reported a last_release in 2022-05 or 2022-06, clustering too tightly across unrelated projects to be real, and guessed at a bulk registry metadata operation. That guess was wrong. Re-resolving showed the dates were simply the day the original lookup ran: the field had been filled with the check date rather than the release date, on 23 of 71 rows. The real dates range from 2013 to 2026, and some of those packages genuinely have not shipped in a decade — which the wrong dates were concealing.
_polled: Registry state as of 2026-08-18, refreshed by scripts/poll-registries.js. Do not hand-edit version, last_release, stars or archived — the next run overwrites them. Licence differences are reported by the poller but never written, because the registry's answer and the catalogue's are not always disagreeing.
